Surely his Lord was ever Seeing of him.﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 15] ﴿So I swear by the afterglow,﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 16] ﴿and by the night and what it gathers,﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 17] ﴿and by the moon when it becomes full,﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 18] ﴿you will surely ride from stage to stage.﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 19] ﴿What then is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 20] ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not prostrate.﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 21] ﴿Rather, those who disbelieve deny it.﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 22] ﴿And Allah knows best what they conceal.﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 23] ﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment,﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 24] ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds; for them is a reward never to be cut off.﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 25]

Time is nothing but two turns; of them, I die, and another I seek life, toiling.

And another said:

The cheerfulness of every good life has passed away, and I remain toiling for life and wearied.

Haara (to return): he went back. The poet said:

A man is nothing but like a meteor and its light; it returns to ash after it was blazing.

Al-shafaq (afterglow): the redness after the sun sets, when the late night prayer ('isha') time comes. It is said that its root is from the softness of a thing; one says shay'un shafaq, meaning it does not hold together because of its softness. From it comes ashfaqa 'alayhi (he felt compassion for him), meaning his heart softened. Al-shafaqah (compassion) is the noun from al-shifaq, and so is al-shafaq. The poet said:

She loves my life, and I love her death out of compassion; and death is the most noble guest for the free.

Wasaqa: he gathered and collected. From it comes al-wasq, the collected sa's, which are sixty sa's. Ta'am mawsuq means gathered food. Ibil mustawsiqah means camels gathered together. The poet said:

Indeed, for us are she-camels, pure-bred, gathered together, which would find a driver if they were to seek one.

Ittasaqa: al-Farra' said: the ittisaq of the moon is its becoming full and level on the nights of the full moon. It is an ifti'al form from al-wasq, which is gathering. One says wasaqtuhu fa-ittasaq (I gathered it and it became gathered). One also says amr fulan muttasiq, meaning his affair is gathered upon righteousness and orderly.

(Tabaqan 'an tabaq): a state after a state. Al-tabaq is what matches another. Atbaq al-tharaa are the layers of the soil that match one another. From this, the cover is called al-tabaq. Al-A'raj ibn Habis said:

Indeed, I am a man who has milked the years to their last drops, and a layer of them drove me to another layer.

Imru' al-Qays said:

A heavy rain, in which there is a flood-layer covering the earth, flows and scatters.

(p-445) This surah is Meccan, and its connection with what precedes it is clear. Ibn 'Abbas said: "inshaqqat" means "tanshaqqu," that is, it splits open with the clouds. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj also said this. It was also said: it splits open because of the terror of the Day of Resurrection, as in His saying: ﴿And the sky will be split open, for it will be frail that day.﴾ [al-Haqqah: 16]

The majority of reciters read the ta' of "inshaqqat" and what follows it with a sukun, both in connected and pausal reading. 'Ubayd ibn 'Aqil, from Abu 'Amr, read it with ishmam of kasrah in pause, after having not differed in the connected reading with sukun. The author of al-Lawami' said: this is one of the changes that affect the rawiy (rhyme letter) in qawafi (rhymed endings). In this ishmam is a clarification that this ta' is a sign of the feminine verb conjugation and is not one of the letters that change in nouns. Thus it becomes a distinction between the noun and the verb for one who pauses on what is in nouns with a ta'. This is the dialect of Tayy, and some ta's in the Mushafs have been written according to it. End quote.

Ibn Khalawayh said: (idha al-sama'u inshaqqat) with kasrah on the ta', from 'Ubayd, from Abu 'Amr. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Abu 'Amr read (wa-inshaqqat), pausing on the ta' as if he gives it a slight touch of the genitive, and so in its sisters. Abu Hatim said: I heard a fluent Bedouin in the lands of Qays who would kasrah these ta's, and it is a dialect. End quote.

That is because the fawasil (verse endings) may be treated like the qawafi (rhymed endings). Just as this ta' is made kasrah in the qawafi, it is made kasrah in the fawasil. An example of its kasrah in the qawafi is the saying of Kuthayyir 'Azzah:

I am not one who calls for 'Azzah's destruction, nor one who gloats that the sandal of 'Azzah has slipped.

And the rest of the poem is like this. Treating fawasil like qawafi in pause is a well-known path, as in His saying, exalted is He: (al-zununa) and (al-rasula) in Surat al-Ahzab. Applying the description to the state of pause is also found in the fawasil.

(Wa-adhinat): that is, it listened and heard His command and His prohibition. In a hadith: "Allah has never listened (adhina) to anything as He listens to a Prophet who sings the Qur'an beautifully." The poet said:

Deaf when they hear good said of me, but if evil is said of me in their presence, they listen (adhinu).

Qa'nab said:

If they listen (ya'dhanu) to a doubt, they fly with it in joy, and they are not those who bury what is good when they hear it.

Al-Hajjaf ibn Hakim said:

I have listened (adhintu) to you for what I heard of your barking.

Its adhan (hearkening) is its submission to Allah, exalted is He, when He intended its splitting. It is like the act of the obedient one: when a command from the one obeyed reaches him, he falls silent and submits, as in His saying: ﴿They said: We come obedient.﴾ [Fussilat: 11]

(Wa-huqqat): Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Jubayr said: "and it has right to hear." Al-Dahhak said: "it obeyed and it has right to obey." Qatadah said: "and it has right to do that." This verb is in the passive form, and the agent is Allah, exalted is He; that is, Allah has made it right (haqqa Allahu ta'ala 'alayha) to listen. One says: "fulan mahqub bi-kadha" and "haqiq bi-kadha," meaning he deserves such a thing. The meaning is that there was nothing in the body of the sky that prevents the influence of power on its splitting, its scattering of its parts, and its annihilation. It was said: it may be intended: "and it has right to split because of the intensity of the terror and fear of Allah, exalted is He." Al-Zamakhshari said: "and it is deserving to submit and not refuse; its meaning is: an announcement that the Being who is All-Powerful must be able to do everything within His power, and that this is right." End quote. In his phrase "the All-Powerful Being" is a hidden trace of Mu'tazilism. How this man is devoted to the doctrine of Mu'tazilism, slipping it into everything he says whenever he is able to!

(p-446) ﴿When the earth is stretched out﴾. Mujahid said: "It is levelled." al-Dahhak said: "It is spread out, its mountains having been flattened." The hadith also has this sense: "The earth will be stretched like a tanned hide of Ukaz, until people have no room except the place of their feet." This is because when a hide is stretched, the wrinkles in it disappear and it becomes flat. So the earth will then be as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿a level plain﴾ (Ta-Ha: 106), ﴿in which you will see no crookedness or elevation﴾ (Ta-Ha: 107).

﴿And it will throw out what is within it and empty itself﴾. Ibn Jubayr and the majority said: it throws out what is in its belly of the dead, and empties itself of those on its surface of the living. It was also said: it empties itself of what is on its surface, its mountains and seas. al-Zajjaj said: and of treasures. This was deemed weak, because that happens at the time of the emergence of the Dajjal (the Antichrist), whereas on the Day of Resurrection it is only the dead that it throws out.

﴿And it empties itself﴾ means: it is free of what was in it, holding nothing of them back. The verb "takhallat" can also mean: it exerted its utmost effort in emptying itself. As one says, "al-karīm takarrama" (the generous man showed generosity): he reached the limit of his generosity and went beyond his natural disposition. Attributing this to the earth is a metaphorical attribution, while Allah the Exalted is the One who brings those things out from its interior.

The response (jawāb) of ﴿idhā﴾ (the conditional particle "when") is omitted. One may supply it as in the Surah al-Takwir or al-Infitar, or as what is indicated by ﴿Indeed you are labouring﴾, meaning: every person will meet his labour. al-Akhfash and al-Mubarrad said: it is ﴿you will meet it﴾, i.e., "when the sky is split apart, you will meet it". It was also said that ﴿O mankind﴾ (al-Infitar: 6) is with the omission of the letter ﴿fa'﴾ (the particle "then"), its estimated form being: "fa-yā ayyuhā al-insān" (so, O mankind). It was also said that ﴿wa-adhinat﴾ (and it has listened) has an added ﴿wāw﴾ (the conjunction "and" used as an extra particle). From al-Akhfash: ﴿idhā al-samā'u﴾ (when the sky) (al-Inshiqaq: 1) is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is ﴿wa-idhā al-arḍu﴾ (and when the earth), with an added ﴿wāw﴾. The governing element of ﴿idhā﴾ according to most of them is the response, either the omitted one they estimated, or the apparent one that was said to be the response. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: some of the grammarians said that the governing element is ﴿insha­qqat﴾ (was split apart). Many of their imams rejected this, because ﴿idhā﴾ is in a construct relation (idāfa) with ﴿insha­qqat﴾, and whoever permits it weakens the construct relation in his view and strengthens the sense of condition. End of quote. We choose this view, and we have argued for its soundness in what we have written. The sense is: the time of the splitting of the sky is the time of the stretching of the earth. It was also said: there is no response for it, since it has been put in the accusative by ﴿udhkur﴾ (remember) as a direct object, so it is not a conditional.

﴿And it has listened to its Lord﴾, i.e., in throwing out what is in its belly and emptying itself. ﴿Insān﴾ (mankind) is meant as a genus, and the division that follows indicates this. Muqatil said: what is meant is al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Asad ibn Hilal al-Makhzumi, who disputed with his brother Abu Salama concerning the resurrection. Abu Salama said: "By Him who created you, you will certainly ride the layers (of the heavens) and you will surely reach the steep pass." al-Aswad said: "Then where are the earth and the sky, and what is the state of people?" End of quote. Muqatil meant that it was revealed concerning al-Aswad, but its meaning is general to the whole genus. It was also said: what is meant is Ubayy ibn Khalaf, who laboured in the pursuit of this world, harmed the Messenger (ﷺ), and persisted in disbelief. The most remote view is that it refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), and the meaning is: you labour in conveying the messages of Allah the Exalted, guiding His servants, and enduring harm from the disbelievers. So rejoice, for you will meet Allah with this deed, and it is not lost with Him.

﴿Indeed you are labouring﴾, i.e., striving in your work, whether good or bad, toward your Lord, that is, throughout your life until you meet your Lord, which is the term of your death. ﴿Then you will meet it﴾, i.e., you will meet the recompense of your labour, of reward and punishment. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: according to this view, the ﴿fa'﴾ (then) is conjoining the whole sentence to the one before it, the estimated form being: "then you are meeting it." What he said is not binding; rather it is valid for it to be conjoined to ﴿kādiḥ﴾ (labouring) as coordination of single words (ʿaṭf al-mufradāt). ﴿So I swear by the twilight﴾: God swears by His creatures, honoring them and directing attention to lessons to be drawn from them. The ash-shafaq (twilight) has already been explained. Abu Hurayrah, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, and Abu Hanifah said: it is the whiteness that follows the redness. Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Abi Najih said: here it is as if, when He joined it to the night, He said that. Ibn Atiyyah said: this is a weak opinion. End of quotation. ﴿And by what it gathers﴾: what it gathers of animals and others, since all of that is gathered together and at rest in the darkness of night. Ibn Abbas said: ﴿wa ma wasaqa﴾ means what the darkness covers over. Mujahid said: what it encloses of good and evil. Ibn Jubayr said: what it drives and carries. Ibn Bahr said: what is done in it, and from this is the poet's saying:

"Sometimes you see us righteous, and at other times we are driven along like the one who is wrapped and bound."

Ibn al-Fadl said: every creature returns to God, meaning the creation finds rest in Him and each returns to what it has seen, due to His saying: ﴿that you may find rest therein﴾ [Yunus: 67].

Umar ibn Abd Allah, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Aswad, Ibn Jubayr, Masruq, al-Sha'bi, Abu al-Aliyah, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, Isa, the two brothers (Asim and Hamzah), and Ibn Kathir read it with the second-person address (ta' of address) and a fatha on the ba'. It is said that this is addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ), meaning: state after state, from the struggle with the disbelievers. Ibn Abbas said: a heaven after a heaven during the Night Journey. It is also said: it is a promise of victory, meaning: you will surely ride the affairs of the Arabs tribe after tribe and victory after victory, as it was and occurred afterwards. Al-Zamakhshari said: it has also been read as ﴿latarkabunna﴾ addressing mankind in ﴿O mankind﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 6]. Ibn Mas'ud said the meaning is: you will surely ride the heaven in the terrors of the Resurrection, state after state, when it will be like molten metal and like oil-dregs, and it will split and be rent. Here the ta' is for the feminine, and it is information about the heaven and what happens to it, and the subject pronoun refers to the heaven.

Umar and Ibn Abbas also read it with the ya' from below and a fatha on the ba', using the third-person (absent) form. Ibn Abbas said: it means your Prophet (ﷺ). It is also said the absent pronoun refers to the moon, because it changes its states: from concealment, to the new crescent, to full moon.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿layarkabanna al-insanu﴾ (mankind will surely ride). Umar, Ibn Abbas, Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, al-A'mash, and the rest of the seven readers read it with the ta' of address and a damma on the ba': that is, ﴿you, O mankind, will surely ride﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿latarkabunna﴾ with a damma is addressed to the species, since the vocative is for the species. So the meaning is: you will surely face the hardships: death, resurrection, and reckoning, state after state. Or the states are from the drop of semen to old age, as you say: one stratum after another. Ikrimah said something similar. It is also said that ʿan here comes with the meaning of ba'd (after). It is also said the meaning is: you will surely undergo these states generation after generation. From this is the saying of al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib about the Messenger of God (ﷺ):

"When you were born, the earth shone, and the horizon was brightened by your light.
You were moved from loin to womb; when one age passed, another stratum appeared."

Ibn Bahr said: what is done in it, and from this is the poet's saying:

"Sometimes you see us righteous, and at other times we are driven along like the one who is wrapped and bound."

Ibn al-Fadl said: every creature returns to God, meaning the creation finds rest in Him and each returns to what it has seen, due to His saying: ﴿that you may find rest therein﴾ [Yunus: 67].

Umar ibn Abd Allah, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Aswad, Ibn Jubayr, Masruq, al-Sha'bi, Abu al-Aliyah, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, Isa, the two brothers (Asim and Hamzah), and Ibn Kathir read it with the second-person address (ta' of address) and a fatha on the ba'. It is said that this is addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ), meaning: state after state, from the struggle with the disbelievers. Ibn Abbas said: a heaven after a heaven during the Night Journey. It is also said: it is a promise of victory, meaning: you will surely ride the affairs of the Arabs tribe after tribe and victory after victory, as it was and occurred afterwards. Al-Zamakhshari said: it has also been read as ﴿latarkabunna﴾ addressing mankind in ﴿O mankind﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 6]. Ibn Mas'ud said the meaning is: you will surely ride the heaven in the terrors of the Resurrection, state after state, when it will be like molten metal and like oil-dregs, and it will split and be rent. Here the ta' is for the feminine, and it is information about the heaven and what happens to it, and the subject pronoun refers to the heaven.

Umar and Ibn Abbas also read it with the ya' from below and a fatha on the ba', using the third-person (absent) form. Ibn Abbas said: it means your Prophet (ﷺ). It is also said the absent pronoun refers to the moon, because it changes its states: from concealment, to the new crescent, to full moon.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿layarkabanna al-insanu﴾ (mankind will surely ride). Umar, Ibn Abbas, Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, al-A'mash, and the rest of the seven readers read it with the ta' of address and a damma on the ba': that is, ﴿you, O mankind, will surely ride﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿latarkabunna﴾ with a damma is addressed to the species, since the vocative is for the species. So the meaning is: you will surely face the hardships: death, resurrection, and reckoning, state after state. Or the states are from the drop of semen to old age, as you say: one stratum after another. Ikrimah said something similar. It is also said that ʿan here comes with the meaning of ba'd (after). It is also said the meaning is: you will surely undergo these states generation after generation. From this is the saying of al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib about the Messenger of God (ﷺ):

"When you were born, the earth shone, and the horizon was brightened by your light.
You were moved from loin to womb; when one age passed, another stratum appeared."

Makhul and Abu Ubaydah said: the meaning is: you will surely follow the ways of those before you. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is: you will surely ride the Hereafter after the first life. Umar also read it as ﴿layarkabanna﴾ with the ya' of the absent and a damma on the ba': it is said he meant the disbelievers, and the rebuke that follows is an explanation of this: they will ride state after state of humiliation and abasement in this world and the Hereafter. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas read ﴿latirkabanna﴾ with a kasra on the ta', which is the dialect of Tamim. It is said the address is to the Messenger (ﷺ). It is also read with the ta' and a kasra on the ba', addressing the soul. The thing "tabaqa" in the sense of muṭābaqah (correspondence), because each state corresponds to the next in severity. It is also permissible that ṭabaq be a collective noun whose singular is ṭabaqah, meaning a rank, from the saying of people: they are in strata (ṭabaqat). ﴿ʿan ṭabaq﴾ is in the position of a qualifier to ﴿ṭabaqan﴾, or in the position of a circumstantial (ḥāl) of the pronoun in ﴿latarkabunna﴾.

From Makhul: every twenty years you will find a matter you were not upon.

﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾: an expression of wonder at the absence of their faith, though the proofs have become clear.

﴿And they do not prostrate﴾: they do not humble themselves and submit. Qatadah said this. Ikrimah said: they do not place their foreheads on the place of prayer. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: they do not pray. The majority read ﴿yukadhdhibun﴾ (they deny) with a shaddah, while al-Dahhak and Ibn Abi Ablah read it without the shaddah and with a fatha on the ya'.

﴿What they gather﴾: what they collect of disbelief and denial, as if they were putting it into containers. One says "ʿaytu al-ʿilm" and "awʿaytu al-matāʿ" (I stored the goods). Ibn Zayd said something similar. Ibn Abbas said: what they conceal of enmity towards the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers. Mujahid said: what they hide of their deeds. Abu Raja' read ﴿yaʿūn﴾, from waʿā, yaʿī.

﴿Except those who believe﴾: that is, it had already preceded in His knowledge that they would believe.

﴿Unending﴾: uncut. Ibn Abbas said: ﴿mamnun﴾ means counted against them, reckoned, and tainted by reminding of favors. The discussion of this has been covered in Fussilat. And God is the Granter of success.
